package_info.package_manager: N/A (Java core/runtime, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: All Java versions supporting serialization (especially pre-patched JRE/JDK, vulnerable libraries like Apache Commons Collections, older Log4J, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: The Java deserialization mechanism can be exploited by attackers to execute arbitrary code, load remote classes, or cause denial-of-service by manipulating serialized data streams. Malicious actors craft object streams (gadget chains) that exploit insecure deserialization logic, leading to remote code execution, system compromise, or resource exhaustion. This threat is especially severe in applications that deserialize untrusted data without proper validation or controls.

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Serialized javax.naming.Reference object with remote codebase URL
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, the code leverages javax.naming.Reference to specify a remote codebase URL, causing the JVM to perform a JNDI lookup and load and instantiate a class from a remote server, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading and executing code from a remote location during deserialization enables remote code execution and is a critical security risk. The use of javax.naming.Reference with a remote codebase URL is a known exploitation technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal deserialization should only reconstruct local, trusted objects. Loading remote code via Reference objects is unexpected, unsafe, and violates the principle of local object integrity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI is legitimately used for directory lookups in enterprise Java applications, but it is not intended for loading untrusted code during deserialization, especially from remote sources.
key_indicators: Presence of javax.naming.Reference in serialized stream
Remote codebase URL specified in Reference object
Automatic JNDI lookup and remote class loading during deserialization
Instantiation of classes from attacker-controlled servers

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Gadget chain: ObjectInputStream.readObject() → AnnotationInvocationHandler.readObject() → Map(Proxy).entrySet() → ... → Runtime.getRuntime().exec()
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, a crafted gadget chain triggers a sequence of method invocations, starting from ObjectInputStream.readObject(), passing through AnnotationInvocationHandler and Proxy Map entrySet, and culminating in a call to Runtime.getRuntime().exec() with attacker-controlled arguments, resulting in arbitrary command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserialization should not trigger arbitrary method calls or process execution. Chaining objects to reach Runtime.exec() is a hallmark of deserialization exploitation and enables attackers to run arbitrary system commands.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal deserialization reconstructs data objects without side effects. Gadget chains abuse method invocation during deserialization to achieve code execution, which is not expected or safe.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for such gadget chains in deserialization; method chaining to achieve code execution is only used for exploitation.
key_indicators: Use of known gadget classes (e.g., AnnotationInvocationHandler, LazyMap, InvokerTransformer)
Method invocation chains triggered during deserialization
Presence of Runtime.getRuntime().exec() in the call chain
Serialized data containing attacker-controlled command strings

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Serialized array with field array length = INT_MAX (e.g., private int[] ids = new int[Integer.MAX_VALUE])
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, the code attempts to allocate an array of size Integer.MAX_VALUE, causing the JVM to exhaust available memory and crash, resulting in a denial-of-service condition.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unusually large array allocations during deserialization are a classic denial-of-service vector, as they can exhaust system memory and crash the application or JVM.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal serialized arrays have reasonable, application-specific lengths. Arrays with lengths set to Integer.MAX_VALUE or similar extreme values are abnormal and dangerous.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for such large arrays in typical business logic; such allocations are only used for resource exhaustion attacks.
key_indicators: Array length set to Integer.MAX_VALUE or other extreme values in serialized data
Deserialization triggers OutOfMemoryError or JVM crash
Serialized object streams with abnormally large array length fields

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious serialized object stream containing a Reference object, gadget chain, or oversized array.
Application deserializes the object stream using ObjectInputStream.readObject(), processing the malicious data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggering of malicious behaviors during deserialization

attack_chain.action: Malicious behaviors are executed: remote code is loaded and executed (snippet_1), arbitrary system commands are run (snippet_2), or system resources are exhausted causing denial-of-service (snippet_3).

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of untrusted data streams using ObjectInputStream or similar APIs
Presence of javax.naming.Reference or similar JNDI-related classes in serialized data
Unexpected method invocation chains involving known gadget classes during deserialization
Large or abnormal array allocations (e.g., array length set to Integer.MAX_VALUE) during deserialization
file_indicators: Serialized object files containing javax.naming.Reference objects
Serialized streams with class signatures of known gadget classes (e.g., AnnotationInvocationHandler, LazyMap, InvokerTransformer)
Serialized arrays with extremely large declared lengths (e.g., Integer.MAX_VALUE)
network_indicators: Outbound JNDI lookups to remote LDAP or RMI servers during deserialization
Unexpected network requests initiated during deserialization processing
Connections to attacker-controlled domains or IPs for remote class loading
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deserialization of untrusted or externally-supplied data, especially when the data contains references to javax.naming.Reference or known gadget classes. Flag serialized arrays with abnormally large lengths. Detect outbound JNDI lookups or remote class loading attempts during deserialization. Use static analysis to identify code paths where ObjectInputStream.readObject() or similar APIs are used on untrusted input, and dynamic analysis to observe network activity or resource exhaustion during deserialization.
